subject: physics_ib
source: Podstawa programowa kształcenia ogólnego dla liceum ogólnokształcącego i technikum, fizyka, zakres podstawowy (Dz.U. 2018 poz. 467); klasa 1: wymagania przekrojowe, mechanika, grawitacja, wstęp do termodynamiki; pęd wg IB DP Physics guide 2025 (A.2)

items.question: What is the SI base unit of mass?
items.explanation: The kilogram is one of the seven SI base units; the gram is not a base unit.

items.question: Express the newton (N) in SI base units.
items.explanation: From F = m · a: mass in kg times acceleration in m/s^2.

items.question: Express the joule (J) in SI base units.
items.explanation: Work = force × distance, so 1 J = 1 N · m = 1 kg · m^2/s^2.

items.question: What power of ten does the prefix kilo- (k) represent?
What power of ten does the prefix micro- (μ) represent?
items.explanation: 1 μm = 0.000001 m; the order is milli (10^-3), micro (10^-6), nano (10^-9).

items.question: Convert 72 km/h to m/s.
items.explanation: 72 km/h = 72 000 m / 3600 s = 20 m/s; divide km/h by 3.6.

items.question: Is velocity a scalar or a vector quantity?
items.explanation: Velocity has magnitude and direction; speed is the corresponding scalar.

items.question: Which two of these are scalar quantities: force, mass, displacement, time?
items.explanation: Force and displacement have a direction, so they are vectors; mass and time are scalars.

items.text: The final result of a repeated measurement is taken as the {{mean/average/arithmetic mean}} of the individual readings.
items.explanation: Averaging several readings reduces the effect of random errors.

items.question: A length is measured as 12.3 cm with an uncertainty of 0.1 cm. Write the result with its uncertainty.
items.explanation: A measurement result is written as value ± uncertainty, followed by the unit.

items.question: Round 9.80665 to three significant figures.
items.explanation: The fourth significant figure is 6, so the third is rounded up: 9.81.

items.question: Estimate the height of a classroom door to one significant figure, in metres.
items.explanation: An estimate is a rough but reasonable value, here about 2 m (order of magnitude 10^0 m).

items.question: What is the name of the line along which a body moves?
items.explanation: The trajectory (path) is the set of positions the body passes through; its length is the distance travelled.

items.text: The length of the path travelled by a body is called the {{distance/distance travelled}}, a scalar quantity.
items.explanation: Distance is the length of the trajectory; displacement is the vector from start to finish.

items.question: A runner completes one full 400 m lap of a track. What is the magnitude of her displacement?
items.explanation: Displacement is the vector from the initial to the final position; after a full lap they coincide.

items.question: What is the SI unit of acceleration?
items.explanation: Acceleration is the change of velocity (m/s) per unit time (s).

items.text: Average velocity is defined as {{displacement}} divided by the time taken.
items.explanation: Average speed uses distance; average velocity uses displacement.

items.question: Give the formula for acceleration in terms of change of velocity Δv and time Δt.
items.explanation: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity; its direction is the direction of Δv.

items.question: What does the gradient (slope) of a position–time graph represent?
items.explanation: Gradient = Δx / Δt, which is velocity; a straight line means uniform motion.

items.question: What does the area under a velocity–time graph represent?
items.explanation: Area = velocity × time = displacement (distance for motion in one direction).

items.question: What does the gradient (slope) of a velocity–time graph represent?
items.explanation: Gradient = Δv / Δt = acceleration; a horizontal line means constant velocity.

items.question: A car moves at a constant 15 m/s. How far does it travel in 8 s?
items.explanation: In uniform motion s = v · t = 15 · 8 = 120 m.

items.question: Give the equation for the distance travelled from rest with constant acceleration a in time t.
items.explanation: For uniformly accelerated motion from rest the distance grows with the square of time.

items.question: A bike accelerates uniformly from rest at 2 m/s^2. What is its speed after 5 s?
A train accelerates uniformly from 10 m/s to 30 m/s in 10 s. What is its acceleration?
A ball is dropped from rest. Ignoring air resistance, how far does it fall in 2 s? (g = 10 m/s^2)
items.explanation: Free fall is uniformly accelerated motion: s = g t^2 / 2 = 10 · 4 / 2 = 20 m.

items.question: A stone is thrown vertically upwards at 15 m/s. How long does it take to reach the highest point? (g = 10 m/s^2)
items.explanation: At the top v = 0, so t = v0 / g = 15 / 10 = 1.5 s.

items.question: What is the SI unit of frequency?
items.explanation: 1 Hz = 1 cycle per second; frequency f = 1 / T.

items.question: A wheel completes one revolution every 0.5 s. What is its frequency?
Give the formula for the linear speed of a body in uniform circular motion with radius r and period T.
items.explanation: In one period the body covers the circumference 2πr.

items.question: Two forces of 3 N and 4 N act on a body at right angles. What is the magnitude of the resultant force?
items.explanation: Forces add as vectors: for perpendicular forces use Pythagoras, sqrt(3^2 + 4^2) = 5 N.

items.question: Two forces of 6 N and 2 N act on a body in opposite directions. What is the resultant force?
items.explanation: For opposite directions the magnitudes subtract: 6 - 2 = 4 N, in the direction of the larger force.

items.text: Newton's first law: a body stays at rest or moves with constant velocity unless acted on by a {{net force/resultant force/unbalanced force/non-zero net force}}.
items.explanation: This property of bodies is called inertia; the law holds in inertial frames.

items.question: Give Newton's second law as a formula linking net force, mass and acceleration.
items.explanation: The acceleration is proportional to the net force and inversely proportional to the mass.

items.question: A net force of 12 N acts on a 4 kg body. What is its acceleration?
What net force is needed to give a 1500 kg car an acceleration of 2 m/s^2?

items.text: Newton's third law: if body A exerts a force on body B, then B exerts a force on A that is equal in magnitude and {{opposite}} in direction.
items.explanation: Action and reaction act on different bodies, so they never cancel each other.

items.question: What is the name of the property of a body that resists changes in its state of motion?
items.explanation: Inertia is measured by mass: the greater the mass, the harder it is to change the velocity.

items.question: What is the weight of a 5 kg body on Earth? (g = 10 m/s^2)
items.explanation: Weight W = m · g = 5 · 10 = 50 N; weight is a force, mass is not.

items.question: Which type of friction acts on a body that is at rest but being pushed?
items.explanation: Static friction balances the applied force up to a maximum value; kinetic friction acts on sliding bodies.

items.question: What general name is given to the resistance a fluid (air or water) exerts on a body moving through it?
items.explanation: Drag (resistance of the medium) grows with speed; friction acts between solid surfaces.

items.question: Give an example of a situation in which friction is useful.
items.explanation: Without friction we could not walk, brake or grip objects; it is harmful when it wears machine parts.

items.question: What is the name of the net force acting on a body in uniform circular motion?
items.explanation: The centripetal force points towards the centre of the circle and changes only the direction of velocity.

items.question: Give the formula for the centripetal force on a body of mass m moving at speed v in a circle of radius r.
items.explanation: The centripetal force is proportional to mass and to the square of speed and inversely proportional to radius.

items.question: In which type of reference frame do Newton's laws hold in their basic form?
items.explanation: An inertial frame is one that is at rest or moves with constant velocity; in an accelerating (non-inertial) frame fictitious forces appear.

items.text: A braking bus is an example of a {{non-inertial/non inertial/noninertial}} reference frame: passengers feel pushed forward although no real force pushes them.
items.explanation: In a non-inertial frame we must add fictitious (inertial) forces to use Newton's laws.

items.question: Give the formula for the momentum of a body of mass m moving with velocity v.
items.explanation: Momentum is a vector with the direction of velocity; its unit is kg · m/s.

items.question: What is the SI unit of momentum?
items.explanation: From p = m · v: kilogram times metre per second (equivalently newton second).

items.question: What is the momentum of a 2 kg ball moving at 6 m/s?

items.text: Newton's second law in momentum form: the net force equals the rate of change of {{momentum}}, F = Δp / Δt.
items.explanation: F · Δt = Δp; the product F · Δt is called impulse.

items.question: Under what condition is the total momentum of a system of bodies conserved?
items.explanation: In an isolated system internal forces cancel in pairs, so the total momentum stays constant.

items.question: A 2 kg cart moving at 3 m/s collides with a stationary 1 kg cart and they stick together. What is their common speed?
items.explanation: Momentum conservation: 2 · 3 = (2 + 1) · v, so v = 6 / 3 = 2 m/s.

items.question: What is the SI unit of work and energy?
items.explanation: 1 J is the work done by a force of 1 N over a distance of 1 m.

items.question: Give the formula for the work done by a constant force F acting along a displacement s.
items.explanation: Only the component of the force along the displacement does work.

items.question: A force of 20 N pushes a box 5 m along the direction of the force. How much work is done?
How much work does a force do if it is perpendicular to the displacement?
items.explanation: The centripetal force in circular motion does no work; the speed does not change.

items.question: Define power as a formula in terms of work W and time t.
items.explanation: Power is the rate of doing work (or transferring energy).

items.question: What is the SI unit of power?
A motor does 3000 J of work in 60 s. What is its power?
Give the formula for the kinetic energy of a body of mass m moving at speed v.
items.explanation: Kinetic energy grows with the square of speed: doubling the speed quadruples Ek.

items.question: What is the kinetic energy of a 4 kg body moving at 3 m/s?
Give the formula for gravitational potential energy near the Earth's surface at height h.
items.explanation: Potential energy is measured relative to a chosen reference level (usually the ground).

items.question: A 2 kg book is lifted 1.5 m. By how much does its potential energy increase? (g = 10 m/s^2)

items.text: The principle of conservation of mechanical energy: when only conservative forces (e.g. gravity) do work, the sum of kinetic and potential energy stays {{constant}}.
items.explanation: Friction and drag turn mechanical energy into internal (thermal) energy, so the principle then does not apply.

items.question: A ball is dropped from a height of 5 m. What is its speed just before hitting the ground? Ignore air resistance, g = 10 m/s^2.
items.explanation: m g h = m v^2 / 2, so v = sqrt(2 g h) = sqrt(100) = 10 m/s.

items.question: A pendulum bob at its highest point has 2 J of potential energy relative to the lowest point. Ignoring losses, what is its kinetic energy at the lowest point?
items.explanation: All potential energy converts into kinetic energy at the lowest point: Ek = Ep = 2 J.

items.question: What is the name of the energy a body has because of its motion?
items.explanation: Energy is the capacity to do work; kinetic energy is associated with motion, potential energy with position.

items.question: Give Newton's law of universal gravitation as a formula for the force between masses M and m at distance r.
items.explanation: The gravitational force is proportional to both masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centres.

items.question: By what factor does the gravitational force between two bodies change if the distance between them is doubled?
items.explanation: F is proportional to 1 / r^2, so doubling r gives F / 4.

items.question: What force causes a dropped apple to fall towards the ground?
items.explanation: Free fall is caused by the Earth's gravitational attraction; g is about 9.81 m/s^2 near the surface.

items.question: What force acts as the centripetal force for a satellite in a circular orbit around the Earth?
items.explanation: The gravitational force is directed towards the Earth's centre and keeps changing the direction of the satellite's velocity.

items.text: In a satellite orbiting the Earth, astronauts experience {{weightlessness}} because the satellite and everything in it fall freely with the same acceleration.
items.explanation: Gravity still acts on the astronauts (it keeps them in orbit); they are weightless because nothing supports them.

items.question: What is the name of the state in which a body presses on its support with a force greater than its weight, e.g. in a rocket during launch?
items.explanation: Overload (increased apparent weight) occurs when the support accelerates upwards, e.g. in a lift starting to go up or during rocket launch.

items.question: What is the name of the unit of distance equal to the mean distance from the Earth to the Sun?
items.explanation: 1 AU is about 150 million km; it is convenient for distances in the Solar System.

items.question: What does one light-year measure: time or distance?
items.explanation: A light-year is the distance light travels in one year, about 9.5 · 10^12 km.

items.question: Approximately how old is the Universe according to the Big Bang model?
items.explanation: The Big Bang is the beginning of the known Universe; the galaxies have been moving apart (the Universe expands) ever since.

items.question: What does the observed recession of galaxies (they move away from us) show about the Universe?
items.explanation: The farther a galaxy, the faster it recedes; this is evidence for the expansion of the Universe.

items.question: What happens to the length of a metal rod when it is heated?
items.explanation: Linear thermal expansion of solids; gases and liquids show volume expansion.

items.question: What is the name of the energy transfer between two systems caused by a temperature difference?
items.explanation: Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference; work is energy transferred by a force.

items.text: The internal energy of a system can be changed in two ways: by doing work on it or by transferring {{heat}} to it.
items.hint: energy flow due to temperature difference
items.explanation: This is the first law of thermodynamics: ΔU = W + Q (with the sign convention that W and Q are energy given to the system).

items.question: Which law of thermodynamics is a statement of energy conservation including internal energy?
items.explanation: ΔU = Q + W: the change of internal energy equals heat and work transferred to the system.

items.question: Give the formula for the heat needed to raise the temperature of mass m by ΔT, with specific heat capacity c.
items.explanation: The specific heat capacity c is the heat per kilogram per kelvin; for water c = 4200 J/(kg · K).

items.question: How much heat is needed to warm 2 kg of water by 10 °C? (c = 4200 J/(kg · K))
What is the name of the heat needed to melt 1 kg of a solid at its melting point, without changing its temperature?
items.explanation: During a phase change the temperature stays constant: Q = m · L.

items.question: What is the name of the phenomenon in which two waves overlap and reinforce or cancel each other?
items.explanation: Waves add according to the principle of superposition; crests meeting crests reinforce, crest meeting trough cancels.

items.question: What is the name of the bending of a wave as it passes through a narrow slit or around an obstacle?
items.explanation: Diffraction is most noticeable when the slit width is comparable to the wavelength.

items.question: Which law gives the force between two point electric charges?
items.explanation: F = k · q1 · q2 / r^2: proportional to the charges, inversely proportional to the square of the distance.

items.question: Which law links the current through a conductor with the voltage across it: I = U / R?
items.explanation: Current is proportional to voltage for a metallic conductor at constant temperature; R is its resistance.

items.question: Atoms of the same element whose nuclei differ in the number of neutrons are called what?
items.explanation: Isotopes have the same atomic number Z but different mass numbers A.

items.question: What is the name of a quantum (particle) of light?
items.explanation: Light shows wave–particle duality; the energy of a photon is E = h · f.
